catalog_quote: § 11. Accentuation. ... In Latin the quantity of the penultimate syllable regulates accentuation, as the quantity of the final in Greek. When the penultimate syllable is long, the accent rests upon it; when short, on the antepenultimate, e.g. decóres, décŏres. ... § 12. Syncope of Unaccented Vowels. For a century or two before the literary period the law of accentuation which was mentioned in the last paragraph, the 'Paenultima Law', as it is called, did not prevail. Every word was at that time accented on the first syllable. Long words had, of course, as they had at all periods of the language, a secondary accent as well as the main accent, but in them, as well as in shorter words, the main accent rested on the first syllable. The change to the Paenultima Law of Accentuation began in these long words with the substitution of the main accent for the secondary, the secondary for the main…

new_statements.quote: p. 83: "There is little disagreement that the prehistoric accent of Latin was a stress accent, and that this fell on the first syllable of the word. Its effects are seen in the loss or weakening of vowels in the unaccented syllables, which is typical of strong stress in some other languages" [...] "accent in the senarius in such forms as facilid, cecidero, though this is disputed. But certainly by classical times the principles governing the position of the accent had completely changed in accordance with what is usually called the 'Penultimate Law'. By this, the accent in polysyllables falls on the penultimate if this is of heavy quantity, and on the antepenultimate (regardless of quantity) if the penultimate is light: thus e.g. con-fec-tus, con-fi-ci-o."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for this item has an empty rule field and there are no existing statements; Allen supplies the placement: a prehistoric stress accent on the first syllable, replaced 'by classical times' by the weight-sensitive Penultimate Law, with the Plautine-period evidence (iambic shortening across word boundaries, apud me / pater mi enclitic accentuation) treated as residue of the older initial stress. Compatible with the Lindsay 1894/1922 passages already saved in this folder from the earlier reading (earlier law of accentuation; traces of older accentuation in Plautus). The work is about Latin generally (classical pronunciation), not a separate dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two stages. Pre-literary (prehistoric) Latin: a stress accent fixed on the first syllable of the word, evidenced by the loss/weakening of vowels in unaccented (especially medial light) syllables, and by pre-classical 'iambic shortening' (old Latin ego, cito, modo lightening their final syllable), with disputed traces of the older accent in the senarius (facilid, cecidero). By classical times: the weight-sensitive Penultimate Law (heavy penult stressed; otherwise antepenult regardless of quantity). For the Plautine period specifically Allen only gives the transitional evidence: iambic shortening operating across the boundary of closely connected words in Plautus and Terence (p. 86 n. 1) and enclitic accentuations of the type apud me, pater mi (p. 87).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 86: 'there was also probably a secondary accent (e.g. suspicabar, Carthaginiensis: cf. E. Fraenkel..'; p. 87: in enclitic combinations 'the accent of the main word was maintained, perhaps with a secondary accent on the enclitic'.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics (-que, -ue, -ne, -ce): the grammarians' generalized rule that 'when an enclitic is added the stress always shifts to the last syllable of the main word (e.g. Varro, cited by Martianus Capella, iii, 272..)', while Plautus and Terence show enclitic accentuations of the type apud me, pater mi, extended to idiomatically connected groups (morem gerit, operam..); 'certain peculiarities in the position of the Latin accent' in words originally accented on the penultimate whose final vowel was lost (p. 87); pre-classical iambic shortening / brevis brevians (p. 86); the initial-accent traces in the senarius are marked 'though this is disputed' (p. 83).
new_statements.identity_note: Allen 1978 describes Latin as a whole (the chapter's subject is the classical accent, with a historical introduction on the prehistoric initial stress and remarks on Plautus and Terence); no separate dialect. The oldl1238 item covers the pre-literary and Plautine stages, so only Allen's prehistoric-stress statements and his Plautus/Terence remarks bear on it directly; his Penultimate Law statement is about the classical language.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages (sec. 11 p.25 Penultimate Law; sec. 12 pp.28-29 Early Accent Law with the Plautine fácilius/bálineum residue) are verbatim on the page scan we hold and in the held scanned layer at the stated pages. (2) Deciding source: Lindsay 1915 is an abridged historical handbook, but by the scholar whose 1894 Latin Language and 1922 Early Latin Verse are the primary statements of this account; both now downloaded to and both confirm the classification (1894 pp.157-159: 'the accent should fall on the first syllable of every word' prehistorically; Plautus/Terence facilius, mulierem accented on the first syllable, Paenultima Law otherwise), while 1922 pp.33-34 adds Lindsay's own hedge that the Plautine inference from an earlier reading is 'hazardous' and partly circular. That hedge supports keeping classification weight-hedged/weight-sensitive (tentative) rather than st

sources.citation: Lindsay, W. M. 1922. Early Latin Verse. Oxford: Clarendon Press. (archive.org earlylatinverse00linduoft, scanned text)
sources.quote: 'Quadrisyllables with the first three syllables short seem to have been accented on the first syllable in Plautus' age and for some time later. When precisely the change from, e.g., fámilia to família ... was consummated is hard to say'; Lindsay flags the inference as 'a hazardous discussion which lacks satisfactory evidence and leaves us open to the charge of reasoning in a circle. For we have to take for granted Plautus' regard for Accent', but 'his propensity to place the ictus on the first is unmistakable; and the same may be said of Terence'.
